# Introduction

Here is a citation [@Marwick2017]

# Background

# Methods

## Index design and _justification_ *scoring criteria* 
<!-- I find "justification" not really fitting here and your current version does not indicate that this chapter presents the index in detail. Maybe just "Reproducibility index" would be sufficient as heading here? -->

In order to produce a data-supported description of the current state of affairs, a reproducibility index was designed to check for impediments _or -> for _ data reuse and reproduction in archaeometallurgical studies. Based on the literature review presented above and the common stages of data acquisition, _data_ treatment*,* and analysis in archaeometallurgy, 12 *stages* _phases_ were identified _as potent loci for decision making_ that impact the reproducibility of the methods and output in any given paper *and criteria developed for each stage (see below* _. Below, these stages are described in more detail and pass/fail criteria are described for each_, with examples where illustrative*)*. As a rule, this index focuses on absolute reproducibility, not on the difficulty or ease of the reproduction process. However, the process of testing for reproducibility did yield a number of recommendations for reducing friction in reproduction efforts; these are included below. Furthermore, we combine aspects of data reusability*,* _and_ analytical reproducibility (recording of methods and decisions *related to the analysis*)*,* and computational reproducibility (recording of calculations).
<!-- above: I am not sure if "recording" is the proper term here... -->

These stages are designed as yes/no/not applicable thresholds <!-- not really, aren't they? More accurate would be  yes/partially/no/not applicable, or, to link it closer to the scope: fully reproducbile/partially or with significant effort reproducible/not reproducible/not applicable --> _, and some examples are given below on how these criteria can be met to indicate acceptable standards_ <!-- I would remove this part. You refer to them already further above, which I think is sufficient - or only here -->. <!-- I would move the following sentence to the end of the introduction. This is more "outline of paper" than related to this chapter--> _Best practices and recommendations on how to improve the current state of affairs are discussed further down below._ Due to the inclusion of multiple _sources of analytical data_ *analytical methods* (*e.g.,* _including stable lead_ isotope *analysis* <!-- there are also tin isotopes --> , XRF, SEM-EDS, PIXE, ICP-MS) _and approaches_, <!-- I think this part has to be rewritten to current practice: not all criteria necessarily applied to all publications. The “not applicable” label (translated to a score of 2) was designed to meet those cases -->. A soft fail *, equalling to a score of 1,* _(score of 1)_ was applied for methods for which it is _currently_ not yet common practice to include specific details, such as specifying the use of standardless settings for SEM-EDS or the normalisation *to 100% of EDS and XRF data*. _of the spectrum to 100% for pXRF._ <!-- (it is not the spectrum that is normalised but the quantified results extracted from it) -->

### Stage 1: sampling strategy

To pass this criterion, a paper should first specify the choices made in sampling based on archaeologically informed criteria: which artefacts were sampled (e.g. out of an assemblage), and where on the artefacts were samples taken (especially relevant in the case of composite or repaired objects*)*. Secondly, methodological considerations should also be described: such as how often measurements were repeated per artefact or per location (and if replicates were taken, whether averages are reported or individual readings), and the sample preparation protocol in the lab (or in-situ). This must include the sampling method (e.g. drilling, tweaking, clipping or cutting, etching, abrasion or portable laser ablation), the specific equipment used to take the samples in case of destructive sampling (e.g. tongs, scalpel, or jeweler’s saw), a quantification of the amount of material sampled, the contamination protocols followed and any other sample preparation before analysis (e.g. acid digestion, pulverisation, mounting, pelletizing or polishing [@Westneretal2024]. If no sample preparation was undertaken, such as in the case of non-invasive surface XRF, this should also be explicitly stated.
<!-- Should we split this up into bullet points? This might make it easier to digest as a list of three top-level bullet points (sampling, analytical protocol, measurement) with a second level for the respective criteria. The "measurement" part is missing but at least I checked the entire analytical protocol, including settings such as acceleration voltage, type of inlet system for LIA (spray chamber vs. Aridus), etc. -->

### Stage 2: data availability
Passing the index on data availability can be achieved by having underlying data to a paper attached as supplementary files, embedded in the text as tables or *cited as data publication with the link to its record in a repository* _in a repository_attached via a link to a repository_ <!-- I would actually just write Cited as data publication"... -->. Some of these options may cause more or less friction for the re-user, and we have reflected this in the scoring mechanism. Adding data in tables in the text does quality as reproducible, although it introduces more steps for the re-user when importing the data (resulting in a score of 1). Supplementary data files are preferable in this regard, although here choices regarding file formats were considered, with .csv or .xlsx vastly preferable (and scoring higher) over .docx or .pdf files. As long as all data necessary to reproduce the paper are accessible, a paper should pass this threshold with either a score of 1 or 2. These data could include the raw machine output, processed data or averages of measurements where this is appropriate to the analytical method (as long as the type of data and level of processing is made explicit). A selection of the most significant results does not count as complete. Papers that include a data availability statement that claim all or some of the data are available on request are also considered non-reproducible as data sharing under this provision is neither guaranteed nor enforceable [@Marwick2025].

### Stage 3: availability of comparative data
Many of the papers surveyed contained comparative _analyses of metallurgical_ data <!-- I would write it just like this. Depending on who you ask, chemical compositions ore e.g. lead isotope signatures of ores would not be considered metallurgical -->, whether that was between artefacts from different sites or between isotope signatures of artefacts compared to ore deposits <!-- is "between" here really proper English? -->. In any of these cases, reproducibility of the comparison requires a clear and specific citation to the comparative data used. A score of 0 was given to papers that included no citations or only made general references to these datasets in the text. Higher scores were awarded for citations included in image captions or for papers that reproduced the comparative datasets in full in their own supplementary files. These scores were only given to the presence/absence of clear citations to these data, we did not attempt to track them down and check whether they were accessible according to the criteria set above in stage 2. 


## Crossref search

It was decided to focus this review on recent papers that make an original contribution to the field and that present new compositional, elemental, or isotopic data within the scope of archaeometallurgy. The search was kept to journal articles only, as developments in journal publishing practices have meant publishing (digital) supplementary data files alongside texts has become increasingly common, while still being largely out of scope of printed monographs or edited volumes. Following criticism by *@Marwick.2025* _(references)_, this also enabled us to test compliance with increasingly high standards regarding data availability. <!-- I would rephrase "high standards" here because depending on the view they are not high but the previous state was just underwhelming. Suggestion: ..."to test compliance with increasingly stricter enforcement of data availability." -->

In order to find these publications, _a_ *the* Crossref API _search_ was performed_ *was queried* using the *R-package* **rcrossref** _package in R_ *[@rcrossref]*. The initial aim was to analyse all papers that fit these criteria published within the last year (starting on November 24, 2024, a year from the start of the project). However, it was found that too few papers came through the filters set in the Crossref search (see below) and the search period was extended to _February_ *January* 31, 2026.

The first decision was to narrow down the search scope to a selection of journals that regularly publish papers related to archaeometallurgy. Of the 22 journals originally considered, only *the* 11 *journals listed in tab. 1* yielded significant numbers of relevant papers (based on the initial, shorter, search period) and the others were removed from the filters.

```{r}
create_master_table <- function(start_date = "2024-11-25", end_date = "2026-01-31",
                          journal_issn = source("./analysis/supplementary-materials/journals.R")
                          ){

  results <- rcrossref::cr_journals(issn = journal_issn,
                                    works = TRUE,
                                    filter = c(from_pub_date = start_date,
                                               until_pub_date = end_date),
                                    limit = 1000,
                                    async = TRUE
  )
```

From the resulting output *of 1240 individual papers*, a data frame was extracted using only a handful of columns. The publication date, doi and ISSN of the journal were included in order to keep track of publications while working. Journal title was included so we could gain an insight into different publishing volumes and practices between publishes and article title and abstract (even though not all targeted journals include the abstract in their Crossref output) were included to provide the input for the iterative content filters discussed below. _A total of 1240 individual papers resulted from this initial search._

```{r}
results_data <- results$data[!is.na(results$data$title),
                               c("deposited", "container.title", "title", "issn",
                                 "doi", "abstract")]
```

These were narrowed down using a combination of positive and negative filters to only select papers related to archaeometallurgy, using a selection of search terms appearing in either the article title or abstract. Positive filters for methodology included such terms as “provenance” and “metal”, while negative terms included “genome” and “geospatial”. Positive filters for specific materials were further targeted towards metals, including both alloy types and individual metals. Negative filters aimed at excluding papers on non-metal materials. A handful of search terms for materials were filtered through a masking filter to ensure papers on composite objects or papers that discussed multiple types of material culture were kept in. These filters were all compiled iteratively, meaning *that filters were added and filters term updated as we went through the dataset.* _we repeated the initial broad search multiple times, scanning the article titles and abstracts to identify non-archaeometallurgical papers and adding filter terms as we went to weed those papers out. This process was repeated multiple times before the code was finalised as the current published version._ 
<!-- above: the repeated nature of the process is mentioned twiced. And it might twitch the wrong people if we admit to query the crossref API repeatedly instead of saving a copy of the raw data and carry the filter out on them... further, the same applies to the next paragraph. Hence, I would refer to the code only at the very end (I would also turn them into one paragraph. -->

```{r}
pattern_pos <- paste(

    # general search terms
    "charact", "provenance", "metal", "trace", "element", "isotop", "composition",

    # specific materials or alloys
    "alloy", "bronze", "brass", "gunmetal", "copper", "\\btin\\b",
    "zinc", "\\blead\\b", "\\biron\\b", "silver", "gold",
    sep = "|")

    # Create a vector that selects rows passing the filter and trim dataset accordingly
  filtering_pos <- apply(results_data[, c("title", "abstract")], 1, function(row) {
    any(grepl(pattern_pos, row, ignore.case = TRUE))
    })

  results_filtered <- results_data[filtering_pos, ]

  # This should result in 523 observations

  # Explicitly filter out non-metal materials.
  # The list of terms was compiled iteratively against the dataset
  pattern_neg_mat1 <- paste(

    # search terms related to environmental archaeology
    "soil", "shell", "wood", "charcoal", "bone", "leather", "\\boil\\b", "fibre", "cloth", "silk", "textile", "amber", "crop", "agropastoral",

    # search terms related to mineralogy
    "cinnabar", "malachite",

    # search terms related to stable isotopes
    "strontium", "\\bSr", "86Sr", "carbon", "oxygen",

    # search terms related to ceramic artefacts
    "seal", "amphora", "clay", "pots", "wheel-made", "ceramic", "potter", "porcelain", "cooking", "brick", "paste",

    # search terms related to glass artefacts
    "faience", "glaze", "vitr", "beads",

    # search terms related to stone artefacts
    "graphite", "obsidian", "amazonite", "flint", "chert", "dolerite", "stone", "turquoise", "lime", "steatite", "\\blithic", "-lithic", "rock", "ochre", "marble", "quern", "carnelian",

    # search terms related to plant and animal remains and diet
    "skelet", "weaning", "species", "camel", "horse", "sheep", "pig", "mice", "fish", "animal", "bovi", "cani", "bio", "human", "plant", "food", "diet", "tooth", "dentin", "enamel",

    # search terms related to architecture and building materials
    "architect", "plaster", "paint", "mortar", "inscription", "structure",
    sep = "|")

  # Create a vector that selects rows not passing the filter and trim dataset accordingly
  filtering_neg_mat1 <- apply(results_filtered[, c("title", "abstract")], 1, function(row) {
    !any(grepl(pattern_neg_mat1, row, ignore.case = TRUE))
    })

  results_filtered <- results_filtered[filtering_neg_mat1, ]

  # This should results in 160 results

  # Apply filtering mask to ensure multi-material approaches are kept in
  # The list of terms was compiled iteratively against the dataset
  pattern_neg_mat2 <- paste("water", "fiber", "glass", sept = "|")

  metals <- paste("metal", "alloy", "bronze", "brass", "gunmetal", "copper", "\\btin\\b",
                  "zinc", "\\blead\\b", "\\biron\\b", "silver", "gold",
                  sep = "|") # set filter mask terms

  # Create a vector that selects rows passing the filter and trim dataset accordingly
  filtering_neg_mat2 <- apply(results_filtered[, c("title", "abstract")], 1, function(row) {
    has_neg <- any(grepl(pattern_neg_mat2, row, ignore.case = TRUE))
    has_metal <- any(grepl(metals, row, ignore.case = TRUE))
    return(!has_neg | has_metal)
    })

  results_filtered <- results_filtered[filtering_neg_mat2, ]

  # This should result in 127 observations

  # Explicitly filter out non-metallurgical methodologies
  # The list of terms was compiled iteratively against the dataset
  pattern_neg_meth <- paste(

    # general terms
    "typological", "experiment",

    # methodologies related to environmental studies
    "settlement pattern", "magnetic", "climat", "micromorpho", "geospatial",

    # methodologies related to human and animal mobility, health, diet and death
    "demograph", "organic", "botan", "patholog", "genome",
    sep = "|")

  # Create a vector that selects rows not passing the filter and trim dataset accordingly
  filtering_neg_meth <- apply(results_filtered[, c("title", "abstract")], 1, function(row) {
    !any(grepl(pattern_neg_meth, row, ignore.case = TRUE))
    })

  results_filtered <- results_filtered[filtering_neg_meth, ]

  # This should result in 115 observations
```

The result of these filters was 115 publications, which still included several book reviews, editorial comments and responses to other articles. These were excluded using a separate filter, resulting in 112 articles. The final filter was compiled manually of 19 individual doi’s that were selected after reading the papers from the dataset. Despite the elaborate filters, some papers that were not related to archaeometallurgy had still slipped through, as well as a number of papers that only contained metallographical analyses or papers that did not present new data (such as regional overviews and reassessments of older studies). Although these latter two types of publications are important to our field, and we were pleasantly surprised to see so many publications engaging with legacy data, the focus of this review was on methodological decisions and descriptions, which were less applicable to those types of works. *The resulting R script for querying and processing the publication records was subsequently turned into the function provided in @ASTR_compendium.*

```{r}
  # Create a vector that selects rows passing the filter and trim dataset accordingly

  results_filtered <- results_filtered[filtering_neg_mat2, ]

  # This should result in 127 observations

  # Explicitly filter out non-metallurgical methodologies
  # The list of terms was compiled iteratively against the dataset
  pattern_neg_meth <- paste(

    # general terms
    "typological", "experiment",

    # methodologies related to environmental studies
    "settlement pattern", "magnetic", "climat", "micromorpho", "geospatial",

    "demograph", "organic", "botan", "patholog", "genome",
    sep = "|")

  # Create a vector that selects rows not passing the filter and trim dataset accordingly

  results_filtered <- results_filtered[filtering_neg_meth, ]

  # Filter out publications other than research papers (reviews, responses, comments, editorials) in article title

    "\\(ed\\.\\)\\.|hardback|reply|£|€|\\$|corrigendum|comment|editorial|response",
    results_filtered$title, ignore.case = TRUE)

  ## Manual identification and exclusion of 19 additional papers (total 93) as these concern metallographic analysis only, soil or botanical data or pertain only to regional overview/re-evaluations of legacy data (with no original metallurgical data produced)

      results_filtered$doi)

```

Finally, to create the master table that would form the basis of our dataframe, the results were anonymised by _setting a seed,_ giving each paper a unique *randomly assigned* ID number between 1 and 93 *after setting a seed to make the anonymisation reproducible*, removing all other identifying information*,* and adding _a number of_ columns to store the scores *and additional comments* for each _phase_ *stage* of the *reproducibility* index _as well as additional comments for each explaining the chosen score_. A final column was added as a free field to include comments on the accessibility of the paper. This dataframe was then saved as _a_ *master_raw.csv [@ASTR_compendium, Supplemetary materials]* _included in to the set working directory_.
<!-- we briefly need to define accessibility here. Because it is publications, readers likely think about open access -->

```{r}
 # Set seed for reproducibility and add column 'ID' with random numbers to dataset
  set.seed(42)

  results_final$ID <- sample(nrow(results_final), replace = FALSE)

    # Define columns with identifying information and remove them from dataset
  columns_remove <- c("doi", "deposited", "container.title", "title", "issn", "abstract")
  results_anon <- results_final[, !names(results_final) %in% columns_remove]

  # Add columns for data entry (12 stages of reproducibility index and additional comments)
  columns_add <- c("Stage_1", "Comments_1",
                   "Stage_2", "Comments_2",
                   "Stage_3", "Comments_3",
                   "Stage_4", "Comments_4",
                   "Stage_5", "Comments_5",
                   "Stage_6", "Comments_6",
                   "Stage_7", "Comments_7",
                   "Stage_8", "Comments_8",
                   "Stage_9", "Comments_9",
                   "Stage_10", "Comments_10",
                   "Stage_11", "Comments_11",
                   "Stage_12", "Comments_12",
                   "Accessibility")

  results_anon[, columns_add] <- NA

  # Export anonymised data frame as .csv (; as separator)
  utils::write.csv2(results_anon, "reprod_astr_2026-02-01_anonymised.csv", na = "", row.names = FALSE)
}
```
